prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which brought the measurement of time and frequency to a new level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as my preferred configuration after the full first round. The achievement is a single physical idea with a decisive realisation. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice cancels the differential light shift of the clock transition while holding many atoms free of Doppler and recoil shifts, and Ye's group turned the scheme into the instrument with fractional uncertainty near 1e-18 and, because of the large atom number, very good stability. What followed is a set of measurements of nature that independent laboratories reproduce: clock comparisons at the 1e-18 level, gravitational redshift resolved over millimetre heights, tighter bounds on drifting constants and on dark-matter couplings. From my own work on atomic structure I can say that controlling lattice light shifts, hyperfine mixing and blackbody radiation at this level is not engineering polish, since it rests on understanding the atomic response to a few parts in 1e-18. Answering the chair, I would write the citation narrowly around the lattice scheme and its accuracy, so it is plainly distinct from the 2005 comb prize (a frequency ruler, not a trapped-atom clock) and the 2012 ion-control prize (single quantum systems, not many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength). I would give no weight to the redefinition of the second, which has not happened and should not enter the justification; the case stands on the comparisons already made. Nothing in the first round changed my ranking, but Kroll's and Olsson's points have made me narrower about what the citation should claim.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against is that B041 is the broader achievement: six of eight members prefer it, and it reorganised how condensed-matter physics classifies matter, while clocks improve an existing measurement. I take that seriously and do not dismiss it as a counting matter, but I do not think breadth alone decides it when the credit for B041 cannot be written without a visible gap. The second concern is lineage and credit: the 2005 and 2012 prizes are adjacent, Lemonde, Takamoto, Hollberg and the ion-clock groups are outside the credited pair, and a Katori and Ye split could look uneven given how broad Ye's work is. Third, part of the practical argument depends on a future redefinition of the second. I judge these real but manageable, and none is a scientific objection to the clock result itself. If the committee decides that conceptual reorganisation should take priority this year, B041 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is the configuration I would support, and I would not describe it as wrong.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B041 with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, concedes he has no good answer to the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission, and proposes recording in the deliberation that the HgTe theory credit is incomplete.
responses.response: I appreciate that you state the gap directly, and I agree it should be recorded. But it is the reason I remain cautious: recording that credit is incomplete is not the same as having a defensible allocation. In your trio the gap is wider than the one I raised, since Mele, the joint author of the Z2 theory, is also out, and Mehlig and Olsson have both said that is the weaker choice. I would regard Hasan's ARPES work as a real result, but I would not trade a theory origin for it. With Kane, Mele and Molenkamp the story is coherent, but then Hasan and the 3D chain are left out, and that is a cost the clock pair does not have.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B029 to B041 for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and argues that a three-person topological prize cannot be combined with another part without cutting B041 in a way he would not accept.
responses.response: I agree on the combination point. With a three-person limit, a two-part prize would put clocks and topology in competition for names, and I would not support cutting Kane, Mele or Molenkamp to make room. So this is a choice between single prizes. On your earlier worry that clocks are a refinement rather than a discovery, I accept that you now call that argument weaker. I would only add that the quantity measured, a differential polarisability cancelled at a chosen wavelength and then confirmed by clock comparisons, is a statement about atoms that was not known to be achievable before, which is what I take to be a discovery in the instrument-driven sense.

responses.point: Olsson moved from Hasan to Mele in B041, and argues that the redefinition of the second is a reason to wait for that outcome, while the topological case is already settled.
responses.response: I agree with your move to Mele; it removes the weakest part of the topological configuration. On waiting for the redefinition, I disagree on the logic but not on the facts. The redefinition is a metrological decision that follows from results which already exist, and I would not make the prize depend on it. If we wait for the outcome we reward a policy decision rather than the physics, whereas the lattice-clock comparisons and the redshift measurements are done. Your point does apply if anyone uses the redefinition to argue priority, and I have said above that it should not appear in the justification. We differ in that you read maturity as a reason to give topology priority, while I read it as showing that both are ready.

responses.point: Kroll holds B013 with the same pair, says the citation should be narrow and should not lean on the redefinition of the second, and flags a possible recusal question through the Hall group.
responses.response: I agree with the narrow citation and have adopted it, and with leaving the redefinition out. On your conflict, I think you are right to raise it, and I do not wish to be the one to settle it. It affects how I read the committee's weight on B013: if you are recused from the deliberation, B013 loses one of its two first-place supporters, and I would not want the committee to read the clock case as stronger or weaker for that reason. I accept the shared reservation that a Katori and Ye split could look uneven. My reading is that Katori holds priority on the lattice scheme and Ye on its realisation as a record instrument.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved from B018 to B041 for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, with a deliberately narrow citation that acknowledges the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap, and says the 2016 prize does not overlap.
responses.response: I accept your point on 2016, and I do not rate the overlap as an obstacle to B041; the 2016 prize was about topological phase transitions and the Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz ideas, not about the Z2 insulator or its realisation in HgTe. I also share your sequencing worry from the opposite side: whichever candidate is recognised this year, the other should remain a strong candidate for a later year, and I do not think that argument should decide this year's choice. Where we differ is that you describe the narrow citation as honest and I agree, but the same candour shows that every three-name topological configuration has a stated hole, and I give that some weight.

responses.point: Johansson holds B041 for breadth of consequence, calls B013 a strong alternative with cleaner attribution, and would accept B013 as a fall-back if the topological allocation cannot be settled.
responses.response: Thank you; I think that is a fair statement of where we differ, which is a difference in the criterion and not in the facts. If the committee can settle the topological allocation, your breadth argument is a legitimate one and I do not claim clocks are broader. I would note that your fall-back means B013 is the candidate on which more of us could converge without a compromise, but I do not offer that as a count. I would not ask you to move because of it.

uncertainties: Which criterion should decide between B041 and B013 if only one can be recognised: breadth of conceptual reorganisation or precision of a sharply defined invention. I do not think the scientific evidence settles this for us.
Whether Katori and Ye is the right two-name credit, given Lemonde, Takamoto and Hollberg, or whether it should be read as an incomplete list.
Whether a clock prize this year would be judged too close to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether a recusal of Kroll or a different weighing by the committee changes how B013 should be discussed.
How Ye's separate candidacy under B007 should interact with the clock credit. I recall the priority history from memory and have not verified every claim.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I report no personal collaboration with Katori or Ye in my documented record. My ties are to Anne L'Huillier, the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group at ETH, Reinhold Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato, and none of them are credited on B013, B041 or B014. I am close to B013 by field, as an atomic theorist, which is a field closeness and not a personal connection. Since Kroll has flagged a possible recusal, I note that I have no similar tie through the Hall group.
